questions.stem: What does a mass spectrometer determine for a sample of an element?

options.text: The relative isotopic mass and relative abundance of each isotope
options.explanation: The two outputs the instrument is built for.

options.text: The number of covalent bonds in the sample
options.explanation: Bonding is not what the instrument reads.

options.text: The boiling point of each isotope
options.explanation: Physical properties like boiling point are out of scope.

options.text: The electron configuration of the atoms
options.explanation: Configurations come from ionisation-energy data, not the spectrometer.

questions.stem: Why must the sample be ionised inside the spectrometer?

options.explanation: Ionisation removes electrons, slightly reducing mass.

options.text: Fields can only accelerate and deflect charged particles
options.explanation: Neutral atoms ignore electric and magnetic fields, so no sorting occurs.
Vaporisation happens first, as a separate stage.
No radioactivity is involved.

questions.stem: What role do the electromagnets around the flight tube play?

options.explanation: The detector plate, not the magnets, registers strikes.
Temperature control is not the magnets' job.

options.text: They deflect the ions' paths into curves whose radius depends on mass-to-charge ratio
options.explanation: The field sorts ions by how readily their momentum curves.
Ionisation is done by the electron gun.

questions.stem: What does the detector record for each ion strike?

options.text: A flash of light whose colour is measured
options.explanation: The detection is electrical, not optical.
Temperature is not the detected quantity.
The output is an electronic spectrum, not a print.

options.text: A small current, which is then amplified
options.explanation: Each strike registers electrically and the signal builds the spectrum.

questions.stem: Varying the electric and magnetic fields makes which deflection outcome possible?

options.text: All charged particles, whatever their mass-to-charge ratio, can be swept onto the detector
options.explanation: Sweeping the fields reads out the whole isotopic population.

options.text: The sample is reheated between readings
options.explanation: Vaporisation happens once.
Field variation does not change charges.
The geometry is fixed.

questions.stem: State the five stages a sample passes through in a mass spectrometer.
questions.modelAnswer: Injection and vaporisation, electron-bombardment ionisation, acceleration toward negative plates, deflection in the flight tube's electromagnetic field, and detection as amplified current.

questions.stem: State two applications of mass spectrometry beyond isotope analysis.
questions.modelAnswer: Detecting illegal drugs and supporting forensic science are two; space exploration and carbon-14 dating are further examples.

questions.stem: Explain why the spectrometer reports mass-to-charge ratio rather than mass alone.
questions.modelAnswer: The deflection a field produces depends on both how heavy the ion is and how many charges it carries - a doubly-charged ion curves like a lighter singly-charged one - so the field sort naturally reads the ratio m/z; for singly-charged molecular ions the ratio still equals the relative mass.

questions.stem: In the flight tube, why do lighter singly-charged ions of the same charge deflect MORE than heavier ones at fixed field strength?
questions.modelAnswer: Deflection depends on the mass-to-charge ratio: with equal charge, a lighter ion carries less momentum for the same field to bend, so its path curves more sharply toward the detector.

questions.stem: What defines isotopes of one element?

options.explanation: Isotopes of a neutral element carry no charge difference.

options.text: Equal protons and electrons, different neutron counts
options.explanation: The element stays the same while the neutron count varies.
Different protons would mean different elements.
Neutral isotopes share electron arrangements.

questions.stem: A sample holds 99.76% oxygen-16, 0.04% oxygen-17 and 0.20% oxygen-18. What is Ar to 2 dp?

options.explanation: That reads the middle isotope's mass as the average.
The arithmetic sign of the trace correction was flipped.
The trace isotopes cannot shift the mean that far.

questions.stem: Why does boron's mass spectrum show peaks at masses 10 and 11 in ratio about 20:80?

options.text: Because boron forms B2 molecules in the machine
options.explanation: Element spectra here read atomic ions.
Neither isotope is radioactive.

options.text: Because the 10 peak is an M+1 satellite
options.explanation: Both are isotope peaks, not carbon-13 satellites.

options.text: Boron has two isotopes, B-10 and B-11, with those natural abundances
options.explanation: Peak positions give masses; peak heights give abundances.

questions.stem: What information does the M+ peak of a molecular spectrum carry?

options.text: The compound's relative molecular mass, because m/z there equals Mr
options.explanation: The highest-mass peak is the whole molecule with one electron removed.

options.text: The number of carbon atoms present
options.explanation: That is the M+1 peak's information.
Unrelated to the spectrum.
That is the base peak, a different feature.

questions.stem: Hexane's carbon-13 M+1 peak stands taller than ethane's. Why?

options.text: Because ethane has no carbon-13 at all
options.explanation: Carbon-13 exists at ~1% in every organic compound.

options.text: Hexane has six carbons to ethane's two, and each carbon adds a chance of being carbon-13
options.explanation: The M+1 height scales with carbon count.
Volatility is irrelevant.
Ionisation is single-electron here.

questions.stem: State the weighted-mean equation for relative atomic mass from isotopic data.
questions.modelAnswer: Ar = (abundance of isotope 1 x its mass + abundance of isotope 2 x its mass + ...) / 100.

questions.stem: State the relative atomic mass of boron from its 19.9% / 80.1% spectrum.
Explain why a spectrum can identify propanal rather than butanal.
questions.modelAnswer: The molecular ion peak sits at the compound's relative molecular mass: propanal's CH3CH2CHO+ ion reads m/z 58 while butanal's extra CH2 pushes its molecular ion to 72, so the observed M+ position discriminates the two candidates.

questions.stem: Use the weighted-mean equation to show that boron's Ar is 10.8, given 19.9% B-10 and 80.1% B-11.
A compound containing ONE chlorine atom shows what molecular-ion pattern?

options.explanation: Two isotopes guarantee two peaks.
That is bromine's signature.

options.text: Two peaks, M and M+2, in a 3:1 height ratio
options.explanation: 35Cl gives M and 37Cl gives M+2, matching the isotope abundance.
That needs TWO chlorine atoms.

questions.stem: Where does the 9:6:1 ratio in a two-chlorine compound come from?

options.text: The three peaks' masses add those numbers
options.explanation: The ratio is probabilistic, not arithmetic on masses.
Isotopes do not react with each other.
Fields sort, they do not scale heights.

options.text: The probabilities (3/4)(3/4), 2 x (3/4)(1/4) and (1/4)(1/4) for the three isotope pairings
options.explanation: Each atom is an independent 3:1 draw.

questions.stem: Why does the M+2 peak double in height for the mixed 35Cl-37Cl pairing in two-chlorine compounds?

options.text: The mixed pair can form two ways - 35 then 37, or 37 then 35 - and both land at the same mass
options.explanation: Two routes to one peak double its height.
Its abundance is one third of 35Cl's.

options.text: Because the detector counts it twice
options.explanation: Counting is physical, not double-booked.
They are exactly 2 mass units heavier.

questions.stem: A compound with one bromine atom shows what pattern?

options.explanation: Two isotopes guarantee the doublet.

options.text: M and M+2 peaks of EQUAL height
options.explanation: 79Br and 81Br are equally abundant.
That is chlorine's ratio.
That needs two chlorines.

questions.stem: Bromine's two-atom molecules give a 1:2:1 triplet. What molecular logic underlies the middle peak?

options.text: The middle peak is a fragment, not a molecular ion
options.explanation: It is the genuine M+2 molecular ion.
One compound, three isotope combinations.

options.text: 79Br-81Br and 81Br-79Br both land at M+2, combining to double height
options.explanation: Symmetrically, both mixed pairings weigh the same.
The abundances are equal.

questions.stem: State the peak patterns for molecules containing one and two chlorine atoms.
questions.modelAnswer: One chlorine: M and M+2 peaks in 3:1 ratio. Two chlorines: M, M+2 and M+4 peaks in 9:6:1 ratio.

questions.stem: State the isotope pair and abundance ratio for bromine.
questions.modelAnswer: Bromine exists as 79Br and 81Br in roughly equal abundance, so single-Br compounds show 1:1 M / M+2 peaks.

questions.stem: Explain why halogen-containing compounds are so easy to spot in mass spectra.
questions.modelAnswer: No common organic element else produces these fingerprints: chlorine's 3:1 (or 9:6:1) and bromine's 1:1 (or 1:2:1) molecular-ion doublets and triplets arise directly from the isotopes' natural abundances, so the pattern itself names the halogen and counts its atoms.

questions.stem: Predict the molecular-ion peak pattern, with ratio, for a compound containing two chlorine atoms.
questions.modelAnswer: Three peaks: M (35-35), M+2 (mixed) and M+4 (37-37) in the ratio 9:6:1, from (3/4)^2, 2 x (3/4)(1/4) and (1/4)^2.
